name: Wilson's Stump (Wilson Kabu)

location.address: Jomon Sugi trail, Yakushima, Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan

verify_notes: BLOCKED, not a candidate. This is a dead hollow stump of a Yakusugi cedar felled roughly 300-500 years ago (sources vary: felled c.1586 to supply timber for Kyoto's Hoko-ji Great Buddha Hall, per one account; c.300 years ago per another) at a girth of 13.8m before felling. The hollow interior is about 16 sq m with a spring and a small shrine inside, and a heart-shaped opening overhead when viewed from within. Named after botanist Ernest Henry Wilson, who documented it in 1914. No source describes a living tree growing from the stump's own root system or trunk; three descendant cedars are reported growing NEARBY as separate, independently rooted trees, which is not the same as living regrowth from this specimen (contrast with the Elm of Saint-Gervais precedent, which requires the living successor to BE the entry). This candidate is already recorded blocked in data/leads/yakushima.json with the same finding (re-confirmed there today, 2026-09-04, by an earlier batch of this same famous-trees sweep). No new tree object created; do not ship despite the high demand figure (~990 views/month) per BRIEF_RESEARCH's explicit caution and CLAUDE.md's absolute rule against publishing dead trees as collectible entries.

name: Natural Habitat of Pyrus calleryana (Inunashi/Mamenashi) in Tado
species: Pyrus calleryana var. dimorphophylla, Japanese name Inunashi/Mamenashi (wild pear)

location.address: Near Midori-ike pond, Tado-cho, Kuwana City, Mie Prefecture, Japan

verify_notes: BLOCKED as not a collectible point. This is 'Tado no Inunashi Jiseichi' (multi-do no inunashi natural habitat), a National Natural Monument designated 2010-08-05: a grove/population of 46 mature Pyrus calleryana var. dimorphophylla trees plus numerous seedlings, spread across roughly 3,000 sq m (about 170m east-west by 30m north-south) on the western shore of Midori-ike pond on Tado-yama. This is explicitly an area/habitat designation for genetic diversity conservation of a wild population, not a single named specimen and not a compact ensemble with one obvious place to stand; a viewing/observation trail (Seoto no Mori Course) runs around the whole habitat rather than to one tree. Fails BRIEF_RESEARCH's single-collectible-point rule the same way an avenue or a whole wood does. Reached via Tado Station on the Yoro Railway, about 21.7 km from Nagoya, which would fall outside Nagoya's day-trip cluster in any case even if it qualified as a single tree. Recommend adding to data/leads/nagoya.json as blocked so a future pass does not re-research it.

name: Kawago no Okusu (The Great Camphor of Kawago)
age_estimate: roughly 3,000 years (local tradition, not scientifically dated)

location.address: 7843 Kawago, Wakaki-cho, Takeo City, Saga Prefecture 843-0151, Japan (inside Kawago no Okusu Park)

access: Free to view inside Kawago no Okusu Park, open 9:00-17:00 (an adjacent puppet-theatre attraction, Tameasashikan, may charge separately; the tree itself is not gated). Closed around New Year per the park facility notice.
transport: JR Sasebo Line to Takeo-Onsen Station, then community bus to the Kawago stop, 2 minutes' walk. About 10 minutes by car from the Takeo-Hokuho Interchange via Route 498.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree closely on core facts: national natural monument designated 1924-12-09 (Taisho era), trunk circumference (girth) 21m (2100cm), root/base circumference 33-35m, height approx 25-26m, canopy spread approx 27m in all directions. Ranked among Japan's largest trees by girth (5th nationally per most sources, 'zenkoku kyoju list', though one source says 7th for a DIFFERENT Takeo camphor - see caution below). Hollow main trunk, southwest cavity houses a small Inari shrine stone monument. Legend: Nara-period monk Gyoki carved a 2.4m standing Kannon image into the trunk; the carved image was destroyed in the Meiji-era anti-Buddhist persecution (haibutsu kishaku), but a separate cast-bronze six-armed Kannon found within the tree survives and is a Takeo city cultural property, now kept in a hall nearby (not inside the tree itself). Age of 'over 3,000 years' is a widely repeated traditional/tourism-board figure, not a documented planting date or growth-rate derivation; treat as legendary rather than measured, hence flagged and given a broad band rather than the bare quoted figure. CAUTION for the writer: do not confuse this tree with 'Takeo no Okusu' (Takeo-cho, also Takeo City), a DIFFERENT large camphor about 3-4 km away with its own designation (city-designated 1970, girth ~20m, height ~30m) - the two are easy to conflate in search results and even one of my own source fetches initially returned the wrong tree's page before I found the correct one. Alive and actively maintained: stands in a dedicated public park established 1995 built specifically around this tree, with current visiting hours, parking (~20 spaces) and ongoing tourism-board listings, which is good evidence of continued presence as of recent years; no news of decline or felling found. Coordinates from ja.wikipedia (33.251833, 129.993333) match the candidate brief's coordinates (33.25186, 129.99354) within a few metres, both inside the dedicated park, so location_precision is confirmed. Passes the single-famous-tree destination test: a purpose-built park, national monument status since 1924, and a place among Japan's largest trees together make it a plausible reason to travel on its own, independent of any city.

name: "Senbon Icho" candidate at 31.48857, 130.742443 (Tarumizu, Kagoshima Pref.)

location.address: Shinmido area, Tarumizu City, Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan

verify_notes: BLOCKED. The given coordinates do NOT match the tree the Commons photo filenames point to, and neither form a publishable candidate on its own. (1) The coordinates 31.48857, 130.742443 land on 'Tarumizu Senbon Icho' in Tarumizu City, Kagoshima: a PRIVATELY CREATED ginkgo garden of roughly 1,200 trees planted from 1953 onward by a private owner (Nakaba family) on 4.5 hectares of private land, free to visit seasonally (best late Nov to early Dec, illuminated evenings during a festival). It fails on every count: not ancient (planted within living memory, ~70 years old at most), not a single tree but roughly 1,200 of them, and privately owned (open seasonally by the owner's grace, not a public right of access, so it also sits uneasily with hard rule 10 even though admission is currently free). (2) The Commons photo filenames supplied in the brief (Katsushika-hachimangu, keidai.jpg etc.) point to an entirely different and genuinely remarkable tree: the 'Senbon Icho' / 'Senbon Koson-ju' sacred ginkgo of Katsushika Hachimangu Shrine in ICHIKAWA CITY, CHIBA PREFECTURE, nowhere near Kagoshima (roughly 1,000 km away). That tree is real: estimated over 1,200 years old, height 22m, root girth 10.2m, trunk girth 10.8m, a shrine goshinboku named for the many trunk-like shoots that rose from the base after a lightning strike split the original trunk, designated a National Natural Monument on 1931-02-20 (one of the first in the Ichikawa area), with a white-snake legend attached. This is a famous_trees.py category mismatch exactly of the kind CLAUDE.md warns about (two unrelated things sharing a name): the demand number and photos in the brief likely trace to the real Ichikawa tree while the coordinates trace to the unrelated Kagoshima ginkgo garden. RECOMMENDATION: do not ship anything under this Kagoshima candidate. The real Katsushika Hachimangu ginkgo is a strong candidate in its own right but belongs to a future Ichikawa/Chiba pass, not this Kagoshima-focused batch; record as a lead for that container rather than researched to full ship-readiness here (out of scope, and this pass is already at its four-candidate limit).
